lesson.title: What's Missing: Set Difference
lesson.summary: The - operator (or .difference()) returns the elements that belong to the first set but not the second, and swapping the order changes the answer.
lesson.body:
Set Operations covered union, and the previous chapter covered intersection, which finds what two sets share. Set difference answers a different question: "what does this set have that the other one doesn't." It is the set version of subtraction, and just like ordinary subtraction, order matters. 5 - 3 is not the same as 3 - 5, and set_a - set_b is not the same as set_b - set_a.

The - operator computes set difference in Python, and .difference() does the same job as a method call. set_a - set_b builds a new set containing every element of set_a that does not appear in set_b. Elements that only exist in set_b are ignored entirely, since the question being asked is strictly about set_a's leftovers.

strings_class = {"Alicia", "Bao", "Carmen"}
python_only = {"Deion", "Bao"}

print(sorted(strings_class - python_only))
print(sorted(python_only - strings_class))

The first line prints ['Alicia', 'Carmen']: everyone in strings_class except Bao, who also appears in python_only. The second line prints ['Deion']: everyone in python_only except Bao, who also appears in strings_class. Same two sets, same operator, but reversing the order produces a completely different result. This asymmetry is the entire point of difference, and it is worth pausing on, because intersection and union do not behave this way. a & b always equals b & a, and a | b always equals b | a, but a - b only equals b - a when the two sets are identical.

A natural use for difference is finding what changed between two snapshots of data: which students dropped a course (enrolled_last_week - enrolled_now), or which usernames exist in a backup file but not in the current database. As with intersection, the result is a brand new set, and neither original set is modified by the operation.
